This note keeps **every example, story, study, number, question, and role-play** from the episode, with timestamps. Book: *Conversations* (+ *Cues*, *Captivate*).

## The three levels (Dr. Dan McAdams' framework)

Conversation is not fluid — it moves through 3 distinct levels; you cannot skip to 2 before earning 1. (00:12:14)

| Level | Name | Content | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | General traits | Facts: where from, what do you do, married, kids | Create ease & warmth — a treasure hunt for story, not facts |
| 2 | Personal concerns | Motivations, goals, values, worries | Make someone feel heard; dream-build |
| 3 | Self-narrative | The story you tell yourself about yourself | Understand & potentially rewrite the frame |

**The mental test for level 2:** you're there when you know what gets someone up in the morning AND what keeps them up at night. (00:28:58)
**Diagnostic exercise:** think of the 5 people you interact with most — place each on a level; notice patterns. (00:28:58)

## Level 1 — small talk, done right

### The speed-networking experiment (00:06:53)
3 experiments, 500 speed networkers, cameras in all 4 corners of the room. Good conversation *looks* like: lots of gestures, leaning, high energy, vocal charisma, volume up. Bad conversation: low energy, apologetic facial expressions, low volume. Each networker was assigned 6 conversation starters, rated every timed chat 1–5 (5 = "I want to marry this person / connect on LinkedIn"). Clear winners and losers:

| Rank | Question | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Worst (6th) | "What do you do?" | Socially scripted → autopilot, fact dead-end |
| 5th | "How are you?" | Same script trap |
| **Best (by a lot)** | **"What was the highlight of your day?"** | Not too deep; makes their brain search for optimism; breaks autopilot |
| 2nd | "Working on anything exciting?" | Subtle swap for "what do you do" — reframes work as excitement, or surfaces something better |
| 3rd | "Any fun plans coming up?" | Creates a sense of shared future — we bond with people we could imagine doing something fun with (00:17:03) |
| 4th — **bimodal** | "What's your story?" | People either loved it (5) or hated it (0 — not even on the scale). A level-3 question in disguise: introverts / people who've never framed their story get thrown into cortisol, fight-or-flight. Extroverts default to it — don't. (00:10:23) |

All the winning questions are **"hunting for good"** — inviting the other person's brain to think only about good things.

- **A fact is a stop sign; a story is a doorway.** (00:13:22)
- **"What's your personal passion project?"** — her favorite level-1 upgrade: a hunt for stories and values; if they're married or have kids they'll tell you by accident. Takes conversational courage — safe questions don't serve you. (00:13:33)
- Questions become **callbacks**: "Last time you mentioned X — how's that going?" Being known for better questions means people bring the good stuff to you. (00:17:03)

### Beating the phone feed — "conversational confetti" (00:14:49)
PTA-meeting story: she walked in hoping to meet moms; everyone was scrolling. Lesson: your questions and answers now **compete with the feed** — they must be dopamine-worthy or the brain goes back to the phone.

### Howard Stern — the information gap (00:15:16)
She analyzed thousands of his interview transcripts: his mechanism is creating **information gaps** — "What's the weirdest thing you've ever done?", "The most surprising thing happened to me yesterday — want to hear it?" Superlatives (weirdest, biggest, most embarrassing) open a gap the brain *must* close. Real-life proof: "Guys, the craziest thing happened to me yesterday" → phones down. ("I was stuck in traffic" doesn't qualify — unless you're being funny.)

### Jerry Seinfeld's numbers-based questions (00:24:38)
People meet him post-show starstruck and freeze. His trick: **ask a numbers question** — "How long have you two been together?" → 38 years → "What's been the highlight of your 38 years?" → short → "You're in the honeymoon phase — what's the best part?" Works for introverts and CEOs: fact-shaped opener that jumps to story.

### The no-work party (00:26:00)
A party where the rule was **"you cannot talk about what you do"** (shoes off, successful crowd). Panic → creativity. Her emergent question: **"What do you talk about when you don't talk about work?"** — freedom, discovery, treasure hunt. Level 1 should be approached as a treasure hunt for conversational gold.

### "Tell me something good" — the team ritual (00:22:13)
For teams: once a week, start a meeting with everyone sharing one win — small or big, <3–5 minutes, strictly framed "good" (otherwise people drift to weather/traffic complaints). Creates a safe, timeboxed level-1 space; her team does it on Tuesday calls. Founders who think conversation is anti-productive have it backwards: communication friction → self-doubt, no psychological safety, withheld info, silos. Easy level 1 makes the first 5 minutes of meetings frictionless — people show up on time and want to be there.

### Not toxic positivity (00:23:11)
The goal isn't forced positivity — it's **emotion and story**. If someone answers "I don't have a passion project, I'm going through a hard time" — that's an opening: "Is there anything I can do?" / "Do you want to talk about it?"

### Listening to boring questions — the "what do you do" formula (00:37:02)
- Worst question in the history of conversation: **"Been busy?"** — she wants it deleted from the vocabulary.
- Boring questions asked *of you* are an opportunity: break the script.
- **The coffee-shop eavesdrop (00:38:17):** a date; he answers "I have a system for maximizing achievement in young learners" → she stares → "I work with 5th grade students…" → "Oh, you're a teacher." He gave the brain **too many conversation calories**. The brain wants the easiest road; resume-reading answers turn people off.
- The fix: **what** first, **why/how** second: "I'm a 5th grade teacher — for the last 10 years I've developed a system that speeds up reading." Label first (brain: check, boxed), then the hook.
- **The formula: "I do [what], for [who], by [how]."** Brains need the box; "for who" because listeners are already matching ("can you help my friend?").
- **Multi-hyphenates (00:40:46):** "I daylight as a 5th grade teacher, moonlight as a cinematographer." Career pivot: hero story — "20 years in marketing, thinking about going back for psychology." Conversation can handle complexity.

## The mechanics of turn-taking (00:41:56)

The **Kander Corpus** (huge study of conversation mechanics):
- Ideal turn: **15–30 seconds**; 45s is the ceiling — beyond that it becomes a monologue.
- **Under 15 seconds** = conversational scarcity (not talking/asking enough).
- Self-diagnosis: time yourself on recorded Zoom calls.

Stats she cites (study of 1,000+ Americans, 00:45:28): **95%** have worked with someone who talks too much; chatty coworkers burn **~90 min/day** talking; **71%** say talkative coworkers prevent them getting work done.

### Cues someone wants the turn
- **The "open fish"** — they open their mouth as if to speak (00:00:00, 00:45:53). Steven does this; she stops the moment she sees it.
- No eyebrow raises, no "ooh/ah/wow" → you're not landing. She watches eyebrows like Neil deGrasse Tyson: he claims every book is every eyebrow-raising thing he's ever said — he talks to airplane seatmates and writes down what makes them go "oh". And: "Don't ever get Botox — it'd be so hard to read you." (00:47:04)

### The "do you talk too much" test (01:10:06) — 5 questions; ≥3 "often" = overtalker
1. I leave a conversation realizing I don't know much about the other person.
2. After I finish speaking, people nod politely but don't always respond.
3. I love telling long detailed stories, especially when people are too polite to interrupt.
4. I've been told — gently or not so gently — that I talk a lot.
5. While I'm mid-story, I notice people glance around the room.
All five secretly measure **curiosity**. Steven self-administers on air: rarely / sometimes / sometimes (on stage only — "that doesn't count") / never / sometimes → passes.

### The Yap Challenge (01:11:32)
Open your phone camera, teach something or share an opinion **about yourself**, no notes, hit record. 15–30s natural = fine; 45s = max; 1–2 minutes = you talk too much. On-air demo: "Someone asked my friend out by asking for her Instagram handle, not her number — agree or disagree?" Steven's 12-second answer: "It depends… her vibe, the context…" — tight.

### The Instagram-handle-vs-number debate (01:13:00)
- Steven: Instagram ask is *less invasive* — "I will earn your number."
- Vanessa: **disagrees** — Instagram is performative; pre-browsing it skips level 1, so the first date starts awkwardly at level 2. "Stop asking for handles, ask for numbers." Her deflection if asked: "I have one just for friends and family — maybe you can get there one day." Dating apps get a pass: 6–10 photos and prompts are bounded, unlike an endless years-deep feed.

## Entertainers vs. appreciators (00:51:00)

- **Entertainers:** speak longer, want you to laugh at their jokes, love giving advice, energized by adoration and being listened to. At risk of over-talking.
- **Appreciators:** talk less, love hearing stories, surprise, awe, weird; hesitant to open up; don't want a lot of questions — *tell them stories*. (Both her and Steven.)
- **The green-room story:** a massively famous person (unnamed) in a green room; person after person tried compliment or question — "I love your stuff," "Any advice for a young person?" — flat engagement. Then an **AV guy** came up to mic him: "Can I tell you the funniest story?" — hilarious stories about watching his movies and playing sports with siblings. The star lit up, laughed, and started asking *him* questions. Lesson: he wanted to be **entertained**, not to entertain.
- Practical: with your boss or a VIP, first figure out which type — entertainers get questions; appreciators get stories.

## Conversational narcissism (00:54:34)

- The narcissist walks themselves up all 3 levels — answers their own level-1, tells you their goals, then deepest things you didn't ask for → "verbal vomit."
- Root: **insecurity** + trying to impress. Many know they do it and hate it but can't stop — they're terrified of awkward silence.
- **Her survey (~4,000 people):** greatest conversational fear is NOT rejection or judgment — it's **awkward silences / running out of things to say**. (00:56:03)
- Fixes:
  - **Assertive curiosity** — what/how/why/when follow-ups (not just "tell me more").
  - If invested: "Is it my turn yet? Do you want to hear about mine?"
  - Steven's real case: a friend who over-talks *more* around beautiful women. Her read: he doesn't feel understood/chosen/liked; the quieter Steven gets (out of respect), the worse it gets. Ask better, deeper questions; let them entertain you; see if the insecurity calms.
  - **The bad-driver analogy (01:02:34):** making an over-talker feel like a bad driver makes them tenser and worse. Help them feel like a good driver.
  - **The 9-questions dinner:** "My friend Vanessa gave us 9 questions — want to do them together? I'll go first." Breaks conversational ruts (logistics-only marriages, autopilot friendships).
- **Dream-killing (01:03:04):** smart people accidentally kill dreams by **fact-checking instead of gut-checking** — accuracy-killing a half-formed idea creates conversational scarcity; the other person digs in to convince you. Steven's example: a brilliant interview candidate whose feedback came back neutral/negative — "so obsessed with the pursuit of truth" that connection never happened.
- **Competence without warmth = suspicion** — you can be the smartest person in the room, but if people don't feel connected they don't believe your smarts. (01:04:40)

## Behavioral interviewing (01:06:11)

- "What's your greatest weakness?" → prepared answer. Instead: **"What would your last manager say is your greatest weakness?"** — steps the person outside themselves; bonus: "When I call them, what will they say?"
- Don't ask "tell me about a time you managed a project" (they pick the best one). Ask for the **most recent** — last 2–3 months.
- **Signature questions (the bespoke 6th question):** reverse-engineer what YOU love talking about. Steven loves psychology/behavior → his questions should be "Why'd you make that choice? What made you choose that path?"
  - Amy Poehler's podcast closer: "What are you laughing about lately?"
  - Ginny Urich (1,000 Hours Outside): "What was your favorite outdoor memory?"
  - Vanessa's rotates by book: "Who's the most charismatic person you know?" (Cues era) → "What's your favorite conversation starter?" (now).
  - **AI use case (01:41:08):** if stuck on your character, prompt AI: "What book/movie/TV character is most like me in the way I treat you? I am [mom, entrepreneur, neurotic]. My personality is [x]. My core values are [y]. What character is most similar?"

## Level 2 — dreams, desires, fears

- **Dream building:** everyone has a secret desire / side hustle / passion — help them uncover it. Her live example: she's quietly pitching a TV show. (00:29:33)
- **Pet vs. pest project (00:29:33):** pet = what they dream/hope for (pride); pest = the worry in the attic they want help with but are afraid to ask (shame). Level 2 = making someone safe enough to expose either.
- **Level-2 questions:** "What have you always wanted to learn?" (triggers growth mindset — asking "are you willing to grow with me?"); "What's your biggest goal right now?" — time-anchored: birthdays → "What's your big goal this year?"; January/December → everyone; Steven adds: new quarter, new performance review. Talking about goals dopamine-charges the future self. (00:30:44)
- We've become **embarrassed** to bring private motivation into conversation (journaling/mantras/affirmations are solo); giving permission makes you their ally.
- Dead end? Then **you** answer — or they're an introvert who needs processing time. (00:32:42)
- Taxi-driver scenario: if someone doesn't take the bait, respect it — questions are **bids**, not obligations; "they're not your person or it's not their day." Taxi drivers' own good level-1: "Going anywhere exciting today?" (00:33:12)
- Do you have to *care*? "If you're asking the question, you care enough to try." Leaders who don't feel warm but know they need warmth — intent is enough. (00:35:38)
- Dale Carnegie lineage: **be interested, not interesting**; the most popular kids were the ones with the longest list of people they liked. (00:59:19)

## Level 3 — the self-narrative

- Gate it: reserve for your most important people. **Vulnerability regret** is real — sharing too deep in an unsafe space is soul-crushing. Steven's story: an interviewee spent the first 25 minutes on very early-childhood material; he had to pivot to counselor mode. (01:18:10)
- **Redemption vs. contamination narratives (McAdams):** redemption = "no matter what comes, I overcome" (holds across work, love, parenting); contamination = "everything bad happens to me, I can't get through" — victim of circumstance, unlucky, out of control. Narratives are **frames, not facts** — and changeable; her secret hope is that safe level-3 conversation can flip contamination → redemption. (01:19:17)
- **Narrative hints (01:21:48):** leaks in speech. Contamination: "Everyone always zigs and I zag", "of course, yet another thing", superlatives (always/never), black-and-white, permanent. Redemption: "Good things always happen to me", "there's always a silver lining", "just my luck, I got it."
- Redemption-narrative people **live longer, better immune systems, better connections, happier** — internal locus of control: "I can handle whatever's thrown at me."
- **Locus of control (01:23:25):** internal = agency over decisions; external = worth from outside sources (validation, vanity metrics, likes, invitations). Steven's analogy: **bird vs. roller coaster** — the roller coaster is on a fixed track; the bird has no rail. She wonders aloud whether strong fate-belief correlates with external locus.
- **Fact vs. Frame — the breakup test (01:32:57):** ask about a breakup. Contamination: "It nearly destroyed me; I don't trust men/women anymore; I'm a shell of myself" — permanent. Redemption: "Horrible, one of the worst times of my life — but I know now who to choose. It made me stronger" — antifragile.
- **"Are you lucky?" — the sneaky level-3 question (01:26:28).** Three answers:
  1. Immediate **"Yes"** → gratitude + agency + confidence (speed of answer matters). Steven and Vanessa both say yes instantly.
  2. **"No"** → don't argue them out of it ("think of all you have" = toxic positivity; makes them dig in). Get curious: what forces, when did it change, did you ever feel lucky before?
  3. **"Kind of… / not sure"** → either not introspective (literally never considered it — now analyzing their life on the spot) or you jumped to level 3 too fast / there's shame they're not ready to share. Both are useful data.
- **Richard Wiseman's luck research (01:30:07):** self-described lucky people *generate* their own fortune — lower anxiety, higher extroversion (more contacts), high openness, relentless optimism. There's an academic 10-question luck diagnostic; she's run it in her lab.
- **Luck Labs idea (01:31:24):** a workshop that just harvests feelings of luck — "better than gratitude" (gratitude can shame); feeling lucky is empowering.
- The first-date trap question: would you give a second date to "Are you lucky? — Absolutely not."? She said **no** ("people are gonna be so mad"); on reflection: she'd be curious, but sustained pessimism → not a match, too energy-draining. (01:34:14)

## The five story archetypes (01:35:01)

Fluid lenses on your story *right now* — explicitly **not** Myers-Briggs/Enneagram stable types; "art more than science," harvested from hundreds of narratives.

**Harvesting questions:** "If you had to write a memoir, what would the title be?" · "What book/movie/TV character are you most like — not look like: life choices, personality, core values?" — then **always ask why**. Steven: *The Pursuit of Happyness* — at 18–19 he was shoplifting food, rent 5 months late, swerving landlords; the bathroom-toilet scene with the kid felt like his life; the character goes on to succeed (also: "he's Black"). Vanessa: **Claire Dunphy** (Modern Family) — "people would be surprised I identify first as a mother, not an entrepreneur; a little awkward, very neurotic, constantly struggling with the ambitious-working-mom tension." The critical move: don't assume the character — the *traits they name next* tell you everything, and you probably won't agree with their pick (that's the inconvenient part of level 3).

### 1. Ambitious hero (01:35:32)
Overcomes via grit and resilience; **never satisfied**. Internal monologue: "I got this — hustle — more, bigger, more, bigger." Shiny-object syndrome; work regulates them ("help more people, help ALL the people"); burns out; burns *others* out by dragging them along; accused of hustle culture. Steven's Bezos line: "I have enough ideas to sink the company" — release them at a cadence the company can tolerate; the self-knowledge move is telling your team: "When I come to you with a new idea next week, say no." Conversation tip: they dopamine on goals, progress, metrics — "when someone asks how I am, it takes everything in me not to share my metrics (305% Instagram growth!)"; they love hearing about your growth too — their check-in texts are "how's the biz? how's the traffic?"

### 2. Contented pragmatist (01:42:13)
Likes it as it is; not broken, don't fix; grounded, unambitious by choice; loves habit, ritual, tradition. Annoyed by pushy ambitious heroes. Her real-life example: two people in her life who make "great granola / love smoothies" — she keeps pitching "bottle it and sell it at farmers markets"; they go "…why?" Seen as unambitious; actually content. Relationship risk: the pragmatist partner telling the ambitious-hero founder to "be realistic." Hiring lens: brilliant in **stable, regulated industries** (banking, fiduciary roles — she does finance conferences); "you might want a contented pragmatist running your books"; ambitious heroes get *crushed* in slow-growth environments. Conversation tip: talk ritual, what works, savoring; they make the 3-hour Thanksgiving dinner and want to relive last year, not plan next year. Gift: they remind the hero to "take in the view."

### 3. Selfless helper (01:46:00)
Worth = helping; service careers (teachers, coaches, trainers, nurses, doctors); parents often flip into it on the baby's arrival. Compassion burnout; can't say no; people-pleasers; struggle with boundaries; put themselves last; **attract takers and high-conflict people**. Bill Eddy's high-conflict-person work: ~10% of the population; thrives on drama, black-and-white absolutes, no nuance, weaponizes emotions, sometimes uses psychology as a weapon; worst ones are **enablers** who plant a seed so the helper fights their battle for them. In conversation they deflect ("enough about me — how can I help YOU?") and won't take the ball — talking about themselves feels like *taking*. **The greatest gift: "Getting to know you is not taking from me — it's giving to me. It makes me feel good to hear what's going on for you."** At work: often superb managers (attuned, bring out performance); can be conflict-avoidant — the great ones frame hard feedback as "I'm giving you this because I want you to succeed," and people trust it.

### 4. Creative disruptor (01:51:36)
Her most challenging archetype. Anti-rules; ethos = break things; countercultural; "I don't need a blueprint"; the comments-section people ("this doesn't apply to me because…"); the most outside-the-box thinkers; enjoy negotiating and pushing; **litigators and disruptive entrepreneurs** cluster here. Book example: **Edward Snowden** — wanted to change the system *and* stick it to the man. Steven: "I interviewed one the other day — everything they say is deeply contrarian; having them around refines my own views." They live as **dream killers**: "they'll break you to make you stronger." Prep before seeing one: either "I want to get stronger, be antifragile" or "I'm a delicate flower today — I cannot do the dream-killing." Fine line with pessimism — sometimes they are. Her friend who texts "I hate everything": her Instagram post about him got served *to him* by the algorithm; he texted "is this me?" — "Yes."

### 5. Unlucky struggler (01:51:50 / 01:54:11)
The contamination narrative made person: no matter what, unlucky, stuck, misunderstood, overlooked. Character: **George Costanza** — "everything is bad for me"; hilarious but tortured. Can be very funny, self-deprecating, humble, low self-esteem — "some of the best comedians are unlucky strugglers." The hazard for ambitious heroes: trying to convince them they're actually lucky (that's the toxic positivity trap). Beautiful to be around; you wish they had the confidence you see in them.

## Graceful exits (01:55:48)

**Peak-end rule:** we remember the peak and the **end** of an interaction — everyone engineers the first impression, nobody plans the ending. Formula: **future cue + (compliment OR action)**, delivered in an **exit voice**.

Verbatim role-play #1:
- "Do you have any fun plans coming up this weekend?"
- "There's this wine bar across town I'm really into…"
- "Oh, I hope it's lovely — make sure to try a Chardonnay. **(future cue)** … It was so lovely talking to you — I hope you have a great time at that wine bar. I'm going to go get some more coffee. **(exit voice + compliment + action)**"

Role-play #2 (the counter-question comes back at you): "What have you always wanted to learn?" → if they re-engage, that's what the action half is for — **the action ends it**: "I'm going to go say hi to the host / run to the ladies' room / grab coffee / head home." Then they *cannot* continue.

- **Nonverbal stack:** a slow step back + angling the body toward the door — the brain reads literal disengagement.
- **Be assertive:** the worst last impression is lingering awkwardness ("well… this has been… good"). "The worst kind of last impression is a lingering awkwardness — it is death for charisma."

## Aura, rizz & charisma (01:59:13)

- Her 8-year-old daughter asked "what is charisma?" → definition they landed on: **someone you really want to be around** — you want to sit near them, listen, work, play. Daughter then named 2 kids in her class — the exact 2 Vanessa had already clocked as the charismatic ones. (01:59:34)
- **The basics: be really easy to talk to.** (02:00:45)
- **Be loud with your liking:** "It's always so fun talking to you" / "You always have the best stories" / "You always make me laugh" / "I love when we're put on the same team." Counters **signal amplification bias** (we think our liking is obvious; it isn't) and the **liking gap** (people underestimate how much others like them).
- **Schmobbart, the blind-date suss story (02:01:32):** friends routinely recruit her to vet potential partners. Dinner, Mediterranean platter; the guy was…"okay," no green flags. Next day, before she could deliver the verdict, her friend: "He just LOVED you — thought you were so funny, already bought your Audible book." She caught herself liking him *more* in real time ("He liked my jokes? Really?!") and was horrified professionally — proof of how badly we want to be liked, and how clearly signaled liking compounds.
- **Warmth & competence = 82% of impressions**; every first meeting is two silent questions: *Can I trust you? Can I rely on you?* Charismatic people answer both fast: warm first, then capable/assertive — "I'm going to carry us through this conversation." Having a *plan* is the secret door into charisma.
- **The Austin VIP party (02:05:05):** imposter syndrome; circle intros — "I'm a billionaire and I invented the internet"…"I cured cancer"…escalating impressiveness. Her turn: "I'm Vanessa, I'm a **recovering awkward person**, and I help smart awkward people with my books and my YouTube channel — and I don't know why I was invited to this party." Laughter, a collective deep breath; **every person after her also said "I'm a recovering awkward person."** Post-circle networking: most people came to *her* — not the billionaire, not the curer of cancer — because she was the easiest person in the room to talk to.
- Trying to impress → creates distance. The truly impressive people she's met (billionaires) are humble and downplay success — they've already made it.
- **Master conversationalists are often ambiverts/introverts**, not extroverts — extroverts fall into their own narcissism traps. (02:08:39)
- **Taking up space / winner energy (02:09:04):** the Michelle Obama / Tony Robbins room-entry effect. Studied: winners physically claim more space — more distance between ears and shoulders, torso and arms; **micro**-movements (slight shoulder drop, slight chin up), never arms-up swagger — and it cascades into vocal tone.
- **Maximum resonance point (02:10:41):** the lowest end of your natural vocal range = pride + calm. On-air demo: Steven's "hello" at the top of his breath ("Horrible… embarrassing") vs. hello *on the out-breath* with relaxed vocal cords — instantly more like him. She hears Zoom calls open with breath-held "good morning"s — people give away their vocal competence in the first word. Anxiety tightens shoulders/neck/chin → thinner, faster, breathless voice = "loser feeling"; winners speak on the out-breath and are listened to more.
- **Eye contact (02:13:26):** oxytocin but cognitive load — you can't do complex thinking while holding eye contact (she looks away to remember; give her a math problem, she looks away). Ideal is **60–70%** in Western cultures — not 100, not even 70+. Look away while *processing*; re-engage while *delivering* — because you're simultaneously connecting and reading the face ("do you believe me? are your eyebrows up? is that disgust?"). Front-load eye contact in the first seconds of a greeting for the oxytocin burst, then it's fine to look away.
- **Listening cues (02:16:16):** nodding; the **triple nod**; head tilt (universal warmth — exposing the ear); lean (warm AND competent — literally getting closer to understand); the **lower-lid flex** (competence/intense focus — biological hooding to see detail: "do you see that over there?" → lids harden). When presenting to a C-suite and someone flexes lower lids → **bookmark or pivot** ("dynamic presenting": stop, "does this make sense? any questions? let me give another example"). Cultural note: nodding differs in India, Bulgaria, Pakistan.
- Her friend with the **default disgust face** — a facial *punctuator*, means nothing emotionally; she has to remind herself "he doesn't actually feel disgusted." (02:16:38)
- **Dynamic vs scripted:** don't ask question → check → next question. If "passion project" ignites both of you, spend the whole hour there. "Have a plan, but be dynamic — both can be true." (02:18:44)

## Prep ritual — script your boring questions (02:19:25)

1. Write down the questions you're asked most often (everyone gets a predictable set).
2. Prepare answers that are **gifts to the other person** — story-shaped, inviting "me too / really? / what got you into that?" — not dead-end "interesting facts."
3. Examples: the friend who did 3 years of Bible school — that's the question everyone asks her forever. **Jason**, editor of Entrepreneur Magazine, can't smell or taste — at endless dinners, when "what are you ordering?" comes, he deliberately answers: "Actually I have no sense of taste or smell — if I could taste one thing, what would you have me taste?" → incredible conversations; Nicole Lapin knew him *by that story*.
4. Audit your settings too — if you're always at meals or coffee, have interesting meal/coffee anecdotes ready.

## Closing question + her regret (02:24:22)

The previous guest's card: "Do you sacrifice things in your personal life to build your success that you regret and wish you could get back?" — Yes: moved to Austin for work, left family; doesn't regret Austin, regrets being away from her mom and sister while her kids were very little. "I felt very alone as a new mom… I wish I could get back that time to feel more communal." Now back near family in LA (her sister is at her house with the kids as they speak).

## Skepticism gates

- The speed-networking experiments, "4,000-person" fear survey, archetype taxonomy, and luck-question interpretation are **in-house Science of People research** — most of it unpublished in peer-reviewed venues. Kander Corpus turn-length, McAdams' narrative levels, Wiseman's luck research, Bill Eddy's HCP estimate, the 82% warmth/competence figure, the 95%/90-min/71% coworker study, and the liking gap ARE external published work she's popularizing (she doesn't cite journals on-air — treat exact numbers as directional).
- Archetypes are self-described "art more than science" — memoir-title/character questions are great conversation tools, not psychometrics.
- "1 in 6 people worldwide affected by loneliness" and "only 3 in 10 Americans socialize daily" are quoted without sources on-air.
